title: US Outposts Were Danger Magnets: How Counterinsurgency Trapped Itself
dek: US outposts in Afghanistan were meant to protect villages but became magnets for conflict. The more the military fought, the heavier it got, losing mobility and eventually being trapped by its own fortifications.
why: Wesley Morgan witnessed the Afghan battlefield firsthand and spent a decade researching the deep contradictions of the war on terror: tactical success alongside strategic failure—a story worth pondering for anyone interested in war and organizations.
who: Readers interested in war history, US military tactics, and organizational behavior, especially those curious about the inner workings of counterinsurgency and military decision-making.
skip: The last 5 minutes of chitchat about football can be skipped.

points.body: In the summer of 2010, Wesley Morgan accompanied troops into Afghanistan's Pech Valley and found that US outposts, meant to provide security for villages, actually became "danger bubbles," drawing conflict toward the villagers. Both US forces and the enemy suffered few casualties; the real victims were the villages outside the outposts. This contrast made him start asking: who built these outposts, why, and when—questions that eventually led to his book The Hardest Place.

points.h: The US military grew heavier and clumsier
points.body: From 2006 to 2010, US forces in eastern Afghanistan gradually lost flexibility and mobility, shackled to heavy outposts and MRAPs. In 2006, the 10th Mountain Division could still use pickup trucks and ATVs to reach remote areas, but by 2010, due to the IED threat and top-down force-protection requirements, conventional units could barely get to those places, relying on special operations forces for offensive missions. This overextension meant follow-on units could not sustain the earlier operational tempo.

points.h: Two ODA teams: restraint vs. recklessness
points.body: In 2004, two Green Beret ODA teams deployed to the Pech Valley in succession. The first, from the Utah National Guard's 19th Special Forces Group, used an "ink spot" tactic, trying to build a security zone around the district center, and refused to enter the Korengal Valley because they sensed something there was luring them in. The second, from the 3rd Special Forces Group at Fort Bragg, was eager to enter Korengal to find a fight, but got entangled in a local tribal timber dispute, used as enforcers for one faction, setting off a "snowball" in Korengal that eventually became a fierce, multi-year battlefield.

points.h: Three internal tribes were mutually incompatible
points.body: In eastern Afghanistan, the US military comprised three "tribes": conventional forces, Green Berets (who worked with local partners, training Afghan National Army commandos and local police), and the Joint Special Operations Task Force (e.g., Task Force 373, mainly SEAL Team Six and Rangers, conducting night raids). These three had different goals, sometimes supporting each other but more often getting in each other's way. For example, a task force might kill someone a conventional unit could have easily arrested, and only the task force could reach remote areas conventional forces couldn't. This lack of coordination was a core problem of the Afghan war.

points.h: Commanders measured success with wrong metrics
points.body: Many commanders lacked genuine understanding of counterinsurgency and fell back on quantifiable performance indicators, such as ordnance dropped, miles of road built, or meetings held. The book cites the 2nd Battalion, 503rd Infantry Regiment, which fought in Kunar Province for 15 months, losing 24 soldiers; its commander, Lt. Col. Bill Ostland, defined success by the number of JDAMs dropped, ammunition expended, SERP budget spent, and 10,000 Beanie Babies distributed—metrics that failed to reflect actual effects and were even self-contradictory.

Wesley Morgan points out that many current senior US Navy and Air Force officers have a chapter in their careers that diverges from the conventional path: they led Provincial Reconstruction Teams (PRTs) in Afghanistan's Kunar and Nuristan provinces, including submarine officers, nuclear engineers, and naval aviators. For instance, the current commander of Indo-Pacific Command, Sam Paparo, led a PRT in Nuristan for a year. These missions coincided with the fighting in Wana and Narisan; they went out daily in MRAPs on counterinsurgency missions. This experience became a distinctive mark on their careers.

points.h: Military-media relations went from open to hostile
points.body: Morgan recalls that in 2007, as a 19-year-old freelance journalist, he could almost freely choose which units to embed with, and public affairs officers simply helped him get to company- and platoon-level units. But now, since the embedding program ended in 2013-2014, military-media relations have deteriorated sharply, and a new generation of battalion- and below-level officers view the media as something to be feared. He believes the turning point was not the McChrystal incident but the Obama administration's second term, when the military began restricting embeds, keeping the war out of sight because the uncomfortable truth that "advisors" were really "combat advisors" was unwelcome.

points.h: How Multicam became a mark of the elite
points.body: Morgan tells the story of how Multicam camouflage spread: invented around 2002 by a Brooklyn art school graduate, it lost the Army's competition (the Army chose the ineffective ACU pattern), but Delta Force adopted it privately because ACU performed poorly at night. It then spread through special operations circles, becoming a mark of the elite. Crucially, Crye Precision hinted to game developers that it was the elite camouflage, so Multicam appeared in games like Ghost Recon before real photos, cementing its elite image in young soldiers' minds.

terms.def: Operational Detachment Alpha, the basic operational unit of the Green Berets, typically composed of 12 soldiers.
Provincial Reconstruction Team, a joint civil-military unit established by the US in Afghanistan to handle local reconstruction and governance.
Mine-Resistant Ambush Protected vehicle, an armored vehicle designed to resist IEDs and ambushes.
